paper_title: VidUEU-Agent: A Data-Curation Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Editing, and Unified Tasks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The advancement of multimodal learning is heavily constrained by the scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality instruction data. While raw videos offer an abundant and dynamic source of visual knowledge, transforming them into precise instruction data remains highly challenging. To bridge this gap, we present VidUEU-Agent, an automated pipeline that synthesizes instruction data from raw videos for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent follows a four-stage pipeline: it performs global perception to filter low-quality shots, mines keyframes and multimodal signals, constructs metadata and routes the metadata to synthesize instruction samples. More importantly, our agent framework can autonomously iterate the data distribution based on downstream training results, thereby optimizing data quality, balance, and training effectiveness. Scaling this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K, a large-scale dataset of 100K training samples spanning multiple domains and tasks, providing a robust foundation for developing comprehensive multimodal capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K yields significant and consistent performance gains across diverse representative benchmarks, validating the effectiveness of our proposed agent framework and dataset.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant strides Yin et al. [2024]. These models use vision encoders to bridge multimodal inputs, enabling joint understanding and reasoning Wu et al. [2023], Liang et al. [2024]. Concurrently, multimodal generative models have also evolved rapidly, expanding capabilities from high-fidelity text-to-image synthesis to controllable text-to-video generationZhang et al. [2023], Chen et al. [2025a], Lipman et al. [2022]. However, generative models and MLLMs have progressed along separate tracks, making it challenging to unify understanding and generation in one system Zhao et al. [2025]. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) provide consistent framework for multimodal understanding and generation, showing great potential for multi-step reasoning and controllable image editing Yang et al. [2025b], Chen et al. [2025b], Wu et al. [2025], Deng et al. [2025a]. The advancement of multimodal capabilities relies on the availability of high-quality datasets Yang et al. [2025b]. For UMMs, there remains lack of scalable and reproducible paradigm for producing such high-quality instruction data while minimizing manual annotation cost Yin et al. [2024], Deng 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). et al. [2024]. Raw videos provide scalable source of multimodal knowledge, covering broad domains and temporally ordered interactions beyond static images Tong et al. [2025a]; however, they are also redundant, noisy, and unstructured, and do not directly provide task-oriented instruction data. The key challenge is therefore to convert large-scale raw videos into instruction data that jointly supports understanding and generation while remaining suitable for stable model training. Figure 1: Example samples of VidUEU-100K. We illustrate three capability paradigms: Understanding (top), Editing (middle), and Unified (bottom). In recent years, LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated strong planning and tool-use capabilities, enabling them to decompose complex goals into executable steps and to achieve large-scale data generation, verification, and filtering Guo et al. [2024], Xu et al. [2025], Kumar et al. [2024], Zhang et al. [2025a]. By interacting with external tools and making feedback-driven decisions, agents can automate complex data-curation workflows Tang et al. [2025], Riaz et al. [2025]. These properties make agent systems fit for transforming raw videos into structured instruction data. Motivated by the strengths of agent systems and video data, we introduce VidUEU-Agent, an automated data synthesis framework that leverages agent planning and tool use to convert raw videos into multimodal instruction data. VidUEU-Agent follows four-stage pipeline: it performs global perception to obtain coarse video understanding and filter low-quality shots, mines keyframes and multimodal signals through frame filtering and tool use, constructs metadata from the keyframe sequence and filtered signals, and routes the metadata to synthesize instruction samples for understanding, 2 editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent further autonomously iterates the data distribution based on downstream training results, improving data quality, balance, and training effectiveness. Further, we scale this pipeline to construct VidUEU-100K, large-scale high-quality multimodal instruction dataset built from 8,268 diverse videos collected from the web and open datasets. The dataset contains nearly 20k dense metadata annotations, enabling 40K understanding samples, 30K editing samples, and 30K unified samples, and it spans nine task paradigms and five scenario categories, ensuring comprehensive and balanced data for improving the overall capabilities of UMMs. We further fine-tune series of baseline models on VidUEU-100K and validate the effectiveness of our data through multiple benchmarks and case studies. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose VidUEU-Agent, scalable and automated framework that leverages the planning and tool-using capabilities of agents to synthesize high-quality instruction data for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks from video sources. By scaling this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K, large-scale dataset featuring 20k dense metadata annotations and 100K diverse instruction samples, covering diverse domains and complex tasks across understanding, editing, and unified capabilities. We fine-tune series of baseline models on VidUEU-100K, where extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our data in enhancing model performance in various multimodal tasks.

sections.title: 2.1 Data Construction based on Agent Systems
sections.content: Early methods often used powerful LLMs to directly generate instructionresponse pair Xu et al. [2023], Liu et al. [2023], Zhao et al. [2024]. Despite their efficiency, this approach lacks grounding in verifiable external signals, introducing uncertainty in data reliability and controllability Ji et al. [2023], Rawte et al. [2023], Wang et al. [2023]. Recent trends shift toward vision agents and tool use Gao et al. [2025], Deng et al. [2025b]. Such systems equip LLMs with perception tools for performing complex visual reasoning and information extraction to improve reliability and interpretability Reddy et al. [2025], Deng et al. [2025b]. With this tool-use capability, agent-based data synthesis is becoming promising approach for automated construction of multimodal datasets Sun et al. [2025]. Prior work has explored using model agents to automatically collect bounding boxes, rewrite image captions, or synthesize questionanswer pairs, greatly reducing reliance on manual annotation Chen et al. [2023], Joshi et al. [2025]. LLaVA-Video Zhang et al. [2025b] further synthesizes video-understanding QA from sampled frames, but remains focused on video understanding tasks. However, existing methods struggle to jointly synthesize understanding, editing, and unified instruction data for UMMs, which hinders the development of these models across broader tasks Zhao et al. [2025].

sections.title: 2.2 Multimodal Understanding and Generation Datasets
sections.content: Large-scale, high-quality instruction datasets have become one of the key drivers of recent progress in multimodal models Li et al. [2023], Chen et al. [2023], Liu et al. [2024a]. In multimodal understanding, existing work enhances model capabilities in visual question answering and finegrained recognition Liu et al. [2023], Han et al. [2024], Yue et al. [2024], Chen et al. [2024b], Liu et al. [2024b], Ru et al. [2026]. In multimodal generation, existing work advances high-fidelity generation and controllable editing Zhao et al. [2023], Podell et al. [2023], Cao et al. [2025], Yu et al. [2023], Li et al. [2024]. Recently, the multimodal field has shifted toward unified multimodal models Yang et al. [2025b], Zhang et al. [2026]. Accordingly, unified architectures demand stable generalization across understanding and generation capabilities Tong et al. [2025b], Zhuang et al. [2025], Meng et al. [2026]. However, current image-text datasets are primarily sourced from static images, inherently lacking real-world dynamics Chen et al. [2025c], Shen et al. [2026]. In contrast, videos, featuring inherent temporal dynamics and causal interactions, serve as more promising medium for high-quality instruction data Tong et al. [2025a]. 3 Figure 2: Overview of VidUEU-Agent. The agent performs global perception with quality gating, then conducts keyframe mining using multimodal signals and tool verification, builds metadata, and finally synthesizes instruction data for understanding, editing, and unified tasks.

sections.title: 3.1 VidUEU-Agent
sections.content: We propose VidUEU-Agent, data synthesis agent for raw videos, designed to curate instruction data for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent first parses raw videos through global perception, removes low-quality shots, and then constructs metadata from selected keyframes and filtered multimodal signals. It then maps each metadata entry to suitable instruction data formats, ensures data quality through multi-stage quality screening and consistency filtering, and autonomously iterates the data distribution using downstream training feedback.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Stage 1: Global Perception
sections.content: As preprocessing step, VidUEU-Agent first uses PySceneDetect Castellano to detect shot boundaries and split each long video into sequence of shot-level clips. It then performs global perception at three levels. At the shot level, VidUEU-Agent samples the middle frame of each shot and prompts VLM to generate shot summary. At the chapter level, the agent reviews all shot summaries of the video, groups adjacent shots according to their scene content, maps them into several chapters, and generates chapter summary for each chapter. At the video level, the agent summarizes the whole video based on all shot-level and chapter-level summaries to obtain video summary. Finally, VidUEU-Agent applies Gate A, namely the shot filter, to examine each shot according to informativeness and image quality rules, and removes low-quality shots from the subsequent stages. The prompts for three-level summarization, as well as chapter construction, are provided in Appendix A.1.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Stage 2: Keyframe Mining
sections.content: We perform keyframe mining on the shots that pass Gate A. Frame Sampling. For each retained shot, VidUEU-Agent samples frames at fixed interval and applies Gate frame filtering, which combines tool-based quality statistics with VLM-based check to remove low-quality frames. For each frame that passes Gate B, VidUEU-Agent generates caption. Tool Planning. Based on the 4 Figure 3: Failure Case Examples: Illustrating four common rejected cases in the processing pipeline: Global Rejection, Quality Failure, Gen-Unsuitability, and Task Mismatch. retained frames and the summaries from global perception, VidUEU-Agent performs hierarchical tool planning by assigning tools at both the chapter level and the shot level to collect targeted information. Following this plan, VidUEU-Agent applies the selected tools to every retained frame in the corresponding shot. Frame Scoring and Keyframe Selection. VidUEU-Agent verbalizes the tool signals and scores each frame using these signals together with the three-level summaries. Based on the video duration, VidUEU-Agent sets the keyframe budget and allocates it across shots using the summaries. For each shot, VidUEU-Agent keeps the top-scoring candidates within the assigned quota, computes their image embeddings, measures cosine similarities, and applies weighted facility-location greedy selection to choose high-quality, semantically representative keyframes. The prompts for tool planning, signal verbalization, frame scoring, and quota allocation are provided in Appendix A.2. The tool pool, verbalization rules, and scoring rules are described in Appendix B.

sections.title: 3.1.3 Stage 3: Metadata Construction
sections.content: To construct high-quality metadata and mitigate noise from unreliable signals, the agent first performs specialized checks on the raw multimodal signals bound to the keyframe sequence. For each keyframe, the agent performs specialized checks on the associated signals using predefined rules and determines which signals to retain. Then, based on the keyframe sequence and the filtered signals, it generates transitions describing changes between consecutive keyframes and clip summary that describes the video clip based on the keyframe captions and verbalized tool signals, and verifies the quality and factuality of the generated text using the signals. Finally, it binds the keyframes, their captions, the keyframe-bound multimodal signals, the transitions, and the clip summary to form metadata list for the video clip. The prompts for clip summary generation and pairwise transition generation are provided in Appendix A.3, and the metadata schema is given in Appendix C.

sections.title: 3.1.4 Stage 4: Instruction Data Construction
sections.content: For the generated metadata, the agent applies Gate to perform quality filtering and categorization. Specifically, this gate calls VLM to score metadata by overall information content, logical coherence, and overall quality, outputs decision with reasons about its suitability as instruction data, and removes unsuitable metadata. Subsequently, for each metadata entry, the agent determines the suitable task type(s) and outputs task list with one or more of understanding, editing, and unified. The prompts for task routing and instruction generation are provided in Appendix A.4. Finally, the agent matches instruction templates based on the metadata and its task list, and requires the model to cite the signal IDs used during instruction generation to improve traceability, thereby producing high-quality instruction data. Figure 3 illustrates representative rejected cases across Gate A, Gate B, and Gate C, covering global rejection, low-quality visual inputs, generation-unsuitable frames, and task-routing mismatches. Instruction-data synthesis templates and examples are described in Appendix D, and all quality-control filtering rules are provided in Appendix E.

sections.title: 3.1.5 Autonomous Data Iteration
sections.content: To ensure the final 100K samples are high-quality, balanced, and effective for model training, VidUEU-Agent employs self-iterative data refinement loop. In each iteration, we train models on 30K samples, evaluate them on representative benchmarks, and return results to the agent. The agent reflects on the datas weaknesses, compares new results with the baseline and previous iterations, and updates the target distribution over capabilities, domains, and task types. Under the current policy, the agent adjusts video-type sampling in global perception to prioritize underrepresented types, shifting the domain distribution. In keyframe mining, the agent modifies sampling density and keyframe budget, and adds policy-aware weights to keyframe scoring to align with the desired keyframe distribution. During instruction data construction, task routing adjusts capability and task-type distributions, and quota-based sampling down-samples types whose ratios exceed the target ratios. The agent audits the realized distribution and records statistics, feedback, and policy changes to guide the next iteration. The final 100K dataset is scaled from the Iteration 4s target distribution.

sections.title: 3.2 VidUEU-100K
sections.content: Based on the above framework, with DeepSeek-V3 as the primary agent LLM DeepSeek-AI et al. [2025] and Qwen3.5-9B as the VLM Qwen Team [2026], we construct the VidUEU-100K dataset. It contains 100K high-quality instruction-tuning samples, including 40K understanding samples, 30K editing samples, and 30K unified samples, as well as 20k fine-grained metadata.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Data Collection & Sources
sections.content: Large-scale video sources and scalable agent pipeline enable VidUEU-100K to cover diverse scenarios, including rare and long-tail visual cases. We source videos from large-scale video datasets, including OpenVid-1M Nan et al. [2024] and Panda-70M Chen et al. [2024c], together with videos from Wikimedia and YouTube. To improve coverage in specific domains, we further use specialized open-source datasets such as FineGym Shao et al. [2020], BDD100K Yu et al. [2020], and CodeVidCL Raja et al. [2025]. To build VidUEU-100K, we use 8,268 raw source videos, from which VidUEUAgent derives approximately 8,505 semantic segments for dataset instance generation.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Dataset Composition & Statistics
sections.content: To ensure comprehensive and balanced data, we analyze VidUEU-100K from three complementary dimensions: capability, domain, and task type. For capability, we divide the 100K instruction-tuning samples into Understanding, Editing, and Unified: Understanding covers fine-grained perception, visual reasoning, and multi-image logical consistency; Editing focuses on instruction-based image editing while preserving irrelevant regions; and Unified involves interleaved textimage tasks that require models to understand visual context, infer state transitions, generate target visual states, and select images consistent with the intended change. For domain, we categorize samples into Technology & Tutorial, Sports & Action, Daily Life & Human Activities, Nature & Scenery, and Gaming & ACG. For task type, the agent generates nine categories: Fine-grained Perception, Visual Reasoning, Multi-Image Logic, Editing, Grounded Edit-to-Select Generation, Interleaved Understand RecallGenerateSelect, Stepwise Sequence Generate-and-Select, Middle-Step Gap Generate-andFill, and Instructional Sequential Generate-and-Select. Detailed definitions and distributions of all capability, domain, and task categories are provided in Appendix F.

Overall, these results show that the supervision generated by VidUEU-Agent effectively improves multimodal understanding and generalizes across different model families. Particularly, since MMDU evaluates multi-image reasoning and answer consistency grounded in visual evidence, the MMDU improvements of InternVL3-8B and Bagel show that VidUEU-Agent can mine semantically related keyframes from videos and model their relations in instruction data.

sections.title: 4.3 Results on Editing Capabilities
sections.content: We fine-tune Bagel on the editing subset to evaluate the effect of VidUEU-100K on instruction-based image editing. As shown in Table 2, the data produced by VidUEU-Agent improves Bagel on all GEdit-Bench metrics, reaching 7.565 on G_SC, 7.328 on G_PQ, and 6.951 on G_O, achieving the best results among all com -pared models. These results show that VidUEU-100K improves both edit correctness and output quality, rather than only optimizing one aspect of image editing. The two core metrics reveal consistent but uneven gain pattern. The improvement on G_SC shows that VidUEU-Agent can extract meaningful visual changes from videos and convert them into instructions that guide the target edit more effectively. The larger gain on G_PQ further indicates that video state-transition supervision helps preserve image realism and local visual structure during editing. This is because adjacent keyframes usually share most scene content but differ in specific objects, attributes, or states, matching the edit-and-preserve nature of instruction-based image editing.

sections.title: 4.6 Results on Autonomous Data Iteration
sections.content: We further evaluate the autonomous data iteration process of VidUEU-Agent. Iterations 14 each construct 30K samples and jointly fine-tune BAGEL from the same initial checkpoint before evaluation. The benchmark results are then fed back into the agent, which updates the target distributions across capabilities, domains, and task types for the next iteration. The Final 100K dataset is constructed by scaling the target distribution obtained in Iteration 4, and single BAGEL model is jointly fine-tuned on the complete dataset. Table 4 reports results on MMDU, GEdit-Bench-En, and WEAVEbench, whose aggregate test-split scores guide iteration and constitute development-guided evaluations; full results and feedback-free evaluations on MMBench, MMStar Chen et al. [2024a], and VSI-Bench Yang et al. [2025a] appear in Appendix H. The iteration results show clear upward trend after repeated feedback-driven refinement. Although Iteration 2 slightly decreases on MMDU, it improves on GEdit and WEAVE, suggesting that early distribution updates first benefit generation-related capabilities. From Iteration 3 to Iteration 4, the gains become more consistent across all three benchmarks, indicating that the agent gradually improves the balance among capabilities, domains, and task types. Final further improves upon Iteration 4 with 100K samples.

sections.title: 4.7 Ablation Study
sections.content: We conduct ablations to evaluate key design choices in VidUEU-Agent. Ablations train Bagel on 10K samples per capability; Ours uses separately trained Bagel models on the Final 100K subsets. We separately remove Gate shot filtering (A), Gate frame quality filtering (B), score-and-similarity8 Figure 4: Case study examples comparing baseline models and VidUEU-100K fine-tuned models. based greedy keyframe sampling (S), and Gate metadata filtering (C). We compare with no-agent variant (N) that uses fixed-interval sampled frames as metadata and directly uses VLM to generate QA pairs without tool evidence. Finally, we remove the consistency hard rule (R) requiring each instruction sample to cite used signal IDs. Table 5 reports the main results on MMDU, GEdit-BenchEn G_O score, and WEAVEbench overall score; the full results with the other three understanding benchmarks are provided in Appendix H.4. Baseline dataset comparisons appear in Appendix H.5. The ablation results suggest that all components contribute to performance. Removing Gate causes only mild drop, suggesting that the collected videos contain relatively few meaningless or extremely dark shots after source-level curation. Removing Gate clearly hurts all benchmarks, especially editing and unified tasks, showing that the agent must filter the many low-quality frames in raw videos. Removing score-similarity greedy sampling hurts editing more, indicating that editing data benefits from keyframes that are both informative and non-redundant, rather than from dense but weakly differentiated frame pairs. Removing Gate degrades all tasks, showing that the final metadata filtering step is necessary to prevent inconsistent, incomplete, or task-mismatched evidence from entering instruction synthesis. The no-agent variant drops the most, showing that direct VLM-based QA generation lacks the structured quality control, tool evidence, and task routing needed to construct reliable multimodal supervision. Removing the consistency hard rule also hurts performance, indicating that evidence citation suppresses weakly grounded or low-quality samples.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we study the bottleneck of high-quality instruction data for multimodal tasks, and propose scalable agent-based solution that leverages raw videos as rich and dynamic data source. 9 Specifically, VidUEU-Agent constructs instruction data through four stages: global perception, keyframe mining, metadata construction, and instruction data construction, and refines the data distribution through autonomous data iteration using downstream feedback. Using VidUEU-Agent, we construct VidUEU-100K, large-scale dataset with 100K instruction samples spanning understanding, editing, and unified capabilities. Extensive experiments across representative benchmarks show that fine-tuning baseline models with data produced by VidUEU-Agent brings consistent performance improvements, validating the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed agent pipeline. We hope VidUEU-Agent and VidUEU-100K provide reproducible and extensible foundation for scalable multimodal data construction, and facilitate the development of unified multimodal models that more reliably integrate understanding and generation.

sections.content: A VidUEU-Agent Pipeline A.1 Stage 1: Global Perception The prompts for shot-level summarization, chapter construction, chapter-level summarization, videolevel summarization, and Gate shot admission are shown in Fig. 5, Fig. 6, and Fig. 7. Shot Profiling Prompt You are building visual-only shot profile for video pipeline. Use only the images. Return strict JSON with keys: vlm_summary, shot_role, scene_type, visual_quality_hint, informativeness_hint, candidate_sampling_hint. Allowed hint values for visual_quality_hint, informativeness_hint, and low, medium, high. candidate_sampling_hint: Figure 5: Prompt for shot-level summarization. A.2 Stage 2: Keyframe Mining The implementation prompts and rules for hierarchical tool planning, tool signal verbalization, frame value scoring, and quota allocation with weighted facility-location selection are shown in Fig. 9, Fig. 10, Fig. 11, and Fig. 12. A.3 Stage 3: Metadata Construction The prompts for clip summary generation and pairwise transition generation are shown in Fig. 8 and Fig. 13. A.4 Stage 4: Instruction Data Construction The prompts for task routing and instruction generation are shown in Fig. 14 and Fig. 15. 19 Chapter Construction and Summary Prompts [Chapter Construction Prompt / Pairwise Merge Decision Prompt] You are strict JSON decision engine for merging two adjacent video shots into chapters. Decide whether the two shots belong to the same chapter. Return exactly one valid JSON object and nothing else. Do not use markdown fences. The JSON schema is: { "same_chapter": true, "confidence": 0.0, "hard_boundary": false, "reason_type": "visual_continuation", "notes": "short reason" } Rules: same_chapter and hard_boundary must be JSON booleans; confidence must be in [0.0, 1.0]; reason_type must be short snake_case string; notes must be under 20 words; if evidence is mixed or uncertain, still return valid JSON with lower confidence; base the decision only on the provided shot summaries and hints. LEFT role: <left_shot.shot_role> LEFT vlm: <left_shot.vlm_summary> LEFT scene_type: <left_shot.scene_type> LEFT informativeness_hint: <left_shot.informativeness_hint> RIGHT role: <right_shot.shot_role> RIGHT vlm: <right_shot.vlm_summary> RIGHT scene_type: <right_shot.scene_type> RIGHT informativeness_hint: <right_shot.informativeness_hint> [Chapter Summary Prompt] You are robust chapter summarizer for structured video understanding pipeline. Read all provided shot summaries for this chapter and merge them into one concise, fluent, informative English paragraph. Summarize the chapter as coherent local segment, not disconnected bullet points. Preserve important subjects, actions, stages, transitions, and outcomes; remove redundancy; reflect progression when present; stay grounded in the shot summaries only. Writing requirements: write plain English only; output exactly one short paragraph; do not use bullet points, numbering, JSON, markdown, labels, or quotation marks; keep the summary compact, specific, and easy for downstream planning, scoring, and visualization. Return the chapter summary only. [Video-level Summary Prompt] You are robust video summarizer for structured video understanding pipeline. Read all provided chapter summaries and merge them into one concise, fluent, informative English paragraph. Summarize the global content of the whole video rather than isolated chapter fragments. Capture the overall subject, major stages, important transitions, and final outcomes when supported; remove redundancy; reflect global progression when present; stay grounded in the chapter summaries only. Writing requirements: write plain English only; output exactly one short paragraph; do not use bullet points, numbering, JSON, markdown, labels, or quotation marks; keep the summary compact, globally informative, and easy for downstream planning, scoring, and visualization. Return the video summary only. Figure 6: Prompt for chapter construction, chapter-level summarization, and video-level summarization. 20 Shot Admission Prompt You are strict shot-admission judge for video frame selection pipeline. Judge whether the current shot is worth sending to downstream frame sampling. Keep shots only if they are visually usable and likely to yield informative frames. Reject shots that are mainly low-information filler, weak transitions, visually poor, or not worth spending frame-sampling budget on. Return strict JSON with keys usable_score, quality_score, informativeness_score, decision, reason, evidence. sections.title: Clip Summary Generation Prompt
sections.content: You are writing concise <level> summary for video segment. Summarize ONLY from the provided <level> evidence. Keep it factual, concrete, and short. Return 1-3 sentences only. <level_title> evidence: <evidence_lines> Figure 8: Prompt for clip summary generation. 21 Tool Planning Prompts [Tool Planning Prompt (chapter-level)] You are the chapter-level tool planner for structured video keyframe mining pipeline. chapter is contiguous semantic segment ... usually covering one local topic, stage, or scene block. Your job is NOT to choose frames. for each chapter ... so the pipeline can understand that chapter efficiently ... Your job is to choose the 2 most important tools Planning principles: - Choose the smallest sufficient tool set for each chapter. - Reflect what needed to understand the whole chapter broadly, not every possible detail. - Use the video summary as global context, but judge each chapter independently. - This stage does not decide score_focus. - Reasons must be short, concrete, and grounded in the provided summaries. Output requirements: - Return valid JSON only. - Use English only. [Tool Planning Prompt (shot-level)] You are the shot-level tool planner for structured video keyframe mining pipeline. The video has been decomposed into chapters and shots. Later stages will choose keyframes ... Your job is NOT to choose frames. shot so the pipeline can understand that specific shot ... Your job is to choose the final tool set for each You will be given: - the current chapter summary - the chapter-level recommended tools - all shot summaries inside that chapter Planning principles: - Evaluate each shot independently based on its own summary. - Treat chapter-level tools as recommendations, not fixed final output. - Prefer adding at least 1 extra suitable tool when the shot content supports it; skip only when none is suitable. - Remove chapter-level tool only when it is unsuitable for this shot. - Add only the minimum necessary extra tools from the provided extra candidate list. - Keep the final tool set small but sufficient. - final tool_actions must contain the complete final tool set for the shot, with no duplicates. - score_focus means the 1 or 2 most important tools inside the selected set; it must be subset of selected tools. - Reasons must be short, concrete, and grounded in the provided summaries. Output requirements: - Return valid JSON only. - Use English only. Figure 9: Prompt for hierarchical tool planning. 22 Tool Signal Semanticizer Prompt You are frame-level tool-signal semanticizer for structured video keyframe mining. You will receive multiple candidate frames from the same shot, the tools actually executed for this shot, and each active tools purpose. Your task is NOT to score frames. Your task is to convert raw tool evidence, values, scores, and tool-specific hints into frame-specific semantic descriptions that are faithful to the actual tool outputs and easy to understand. Core requirements: - Be strictly evidence-grounded. - Explain the meaning of tool outputs rather than merely copying raw snippets. - Use tool purpose as context, but base every description on actual per-frame evidence. - Explain numeric values, categorical levels, or structured fields in plain language when present. - Preserve supported directionality, such as stronger vs weaker motion or higher vs lower confidence. - Do not invent thresholds, hidden formulas, unseen objects, actions, relations, or text. - Do not confuse detector confidence, motion magnitude, or tool values with semantic importance. - Use only tools that were actually executed and provided in the input. - For tools not executed or without useful frame-specific evidence, return an empty string for that field. - semantic_text must be short merged frame-specific description from useful active-tool evidence. - Do not score, rank, or compare quality. - Output JSON only. - Use English only. Figure 10: Prompt for tool signal verbalization. 23 Value Scoring Prompt You are frame value scorer for structured video keyframe mining. You will receive multiple candidate frames from the same shot; video, chapter, and shot summaries; the tools selected for this shot and their purposes; score_focus, which names the 1 or 2 relatively more important selected tools; frame-level semantic descriptions rewritten from raw tool outputs; and an extra factual caption for each frame. Your task is to assign one ABSOLUTE value score in the range [0, 1] to each frame. How to reason: - Understand the video, chapter, and shot from the summaries. - Inspect each frames semantic_text, tool-specific descriptions, and factual caption. - Judge what concrete information each source contributes, how clear and specific it is, and how useful it is for understanding the shot. - Treat tool-derived signals as auxiliary evidence; keep the frame caption as central focus. - Integrate all evidence to decide the final score. How to use score_focus: - score_focus is not score dimension list. - When meaningful evidence from score_focus tool is present, give it extra attention. - Do not ignore useful evidence from other selected tools. Scoring principles: - Score each frame on its own absolute usefulness as final keyframe for this shot. - Differentiate frames when they differ in clarity, specificity, or decision value. - Prefer frames that are clear, informative, representative, non-redundant, decision-useful, and easy to interpret. - Reward frames that capture important entities, actions, states, transitions, text, speech-derived meaning, or step-specific evidence relevant to the shot. - Reward frames where caption, semantic_text, and tool semantics reinforce clear grounded interpretation. - Penalize frames that are vague, redundant, weakly grounded, semantically thin, generic, repetitive, or less useful despite technical cleanliness. - Do not treat tool presence, detector confidence, motion magnitude, or other tool-side values as value by themselves. Scoring meaning: - 0.0-0.1: almost no useful evidence. - 0.1-0.25: very weak; evidence is vague, redundant, or not useful enough. - 0.25-0.45: limited; partially useful but missing clarity or informativeness. - 0.45-0.65: moderate; understandable and useful but not especially strong. - 0.65-0.8: strong; clearly informative, representative, or decision-worthy. - 0.8-0.92: very strong; strong candidate for final keyframe selection. - 0.92-1.0: exceptional; unusually clear, information-dense, and highly useful. High-value frames usually clearly show the key subject, state, action, step, transition, result, important text, speech-derived meaning, object evidence, or motion/change evidence; provide non-trivial information beyond generic background or redundant nearby frames; and help justify retaining the frame as representative. Output JSON only. Use English only. Figure 11: Prompt for frame value scoring. 24 Quota Planning Prompt You are hierarchical quota planner for structured video keyframe mining. You must plan quotas at three levels: - global - chapter - shot Goal: Under the allowed total quota range, choose one fixed final global quota and allocate it across shots so later stages can retain the most valuable representative frames. You are not choosing frames directly. Critical planning rules: 1. Choose one integer global_budget inside the allowed total quota range. 2. Do not default to quota=1 merely because there is only one chapter or shot. 3. The sum of all shot target_quota values must equal global_budget exactly. 4. Use video, chapter, and shot summaries to judge where more quota is needed for distinct coverage, richer content, or stronger representativeness. 5. Duration is supporting evidence, not the only reason; longer duration justifies more quota only when summaries suggest broader coverage, multiple stages, transitions, or meaningful states/results. 6. Weak, redundant, or semantically flat shots may receive quota 0. 7. Prefer coverage of distinct stages, states, results, events, or subtopics over near-duplicates. 8. Judge each shot independently while keeping the final allocation globally balanced. How to use the input: - Start from the video summary to understand broad content and final selection coverage. - Use chapter summaries to judge which chapters deserve broader coverage. - Reason shot by shot using each shot summary and duration. - Assign more quota when shot suggests multiple steps, transitions, states, results, or distinct moments. - Assign low or zero quota to weak, repetitive, or semantically flat shots. - Reason fields should explain quotas in terms of summary meaning and coverage need. Output JSON only. Use English only. Figure 12: Prompt and rule for quota allocation and weighted facility-location selection. Pairwise Transition Prompt and Normalization Rules You are analyzing two consecutive keyframes -> from short video segment. Write exactly ONE transition string describing meaningful visible changes from to B. Use images as primary evidence. Captions, video type, global summary, and modality advice are secondary hints; if they conflict with the images, trust the images. Describe only visible changes that affect scene understanding, including object appearance/disappearance, position, state, visible text, camera/view change, or shot change. Ignore tiny flicker, compression noise, blur differences, glare, reflections, and exposure shifts unless they affect meaningful content. Do not infer hidden causes, intentions, or off-screen events. Normalize changes into atomic edits. Each edit should use one target and one allowed verb: add, remove, move, rotate, open, close, turn on, turn off, change text, zoom, pan, tilt, cut. Use image-frame locations such as left side, center-right, upper-left, or bottom center. Avoid object-centric or anatomical left/right. sections.title: RAFT
sections.content: Use recognized textual content as primary evidence for readable text; describe the visible meaning, function, or role of the text rather than enumerating all detected tokens. Reward readable and specific text evidence that reveals task-relevant titles, steps, labels, states, commands, or interface cues; assign higher value when text evidence substantially improves understanding beyond generic visual appearance. Use nearby spoken content as temporal contextual evidence; treat speech as information associated with the frame interval, rather than as on-screen text or direct visual evidence. Reward specific and temporally relevant speech that contributes concrete instructions, explanations, actions, or contextual meaning; assign higher value when spoken content matches the apparent step, state, or action around the frame. Use detected object categories as primary evidence for visible entities; use confidence or location only as supporting information, and describe only entities that are visually supported. Reward clear and relevant visible entities that explain the subject, objects in use, workspace context, or interaction target; assign higher value when detected entities are specific, diverse, and informative. Use optical-flow evidence as primary support for motion or temporal change; interpret motion strength as an indicator of change intensity rather than semantic importance or action type. Reward motion evidence when it marks meaningful transition, interaction moment, or state change; assign higher value when motion helps distinguish the frame from static or redundant neighboring frames.

Figure 26: Prompt for shot admission. E.2 Gate Rules & Prompt After sampling, candidate frames enter two-stage technical quality filter. The fast stage uses OpenCV statistics, including Laplacian variance, brightness, grayscale standard deviation, and histogram entropy, to reject frames with obvious blur, extreme exposure, low contrast, or low 44 informativeness. The model stage uses VLM to inspect higher-level visual usability. The detailed Gate prompt is shown in Fig. 27. E.3 Facility-location Greedy Selection We use standard weighted facility-location greedy selection to choose representative frames within each shot. For each shot, let the candidate-frame set be = {fi}n i=1, and let denote the selection budget assigned to this shot by the quota planner. The goal of RepresentativeSelector is to select representative subset from the candidate set under the constraint k, so that the selected frames cover the important candidates within the shot as much as possible. The objective function is defined as: F(S) = (cid:88) ri max jS sim(i, j), where ri denotes the quality weight of candidate frame fi, and sim(i, j) denotes the similarity between candidate frame fi and the selected representative frame fj. The candidate-frame quality weight is computed from the preceding semantic value assessment: ri = value_scorei. The value score value_scorei is produced by the agent based on semanticized tool signals, while the inter-frame similarity sim(i, j) is computed from the semantic representations of candidate frames. Specifically, the system first extracts image embeddings and caption embeddings, normalizes the visual and textual semantic representations, concatenates them, and then computes cosine similarity: sim(i, j) = cos(zi, zj). During selection, the algorithm starts from an empty set = and maintains the current coverage degree ci of each candidate frame by the selected set. At each iteration, the algorithm traverses all unselected candidate frames fj and computes the marginal gain of adding it to the selected set: (j) = (cid:88) ri max(cid:0)0, sim(i, j) ci (cid:1). The candidate frame with the largest marginal gain is added to S, and the coverage degree is updated as: ci max(cid:0)ci, sim(i, j)(cid:1). This process is repeated until the shot-level budget is reached or all candidate frames have been exhausted. E.4 Signal Filtering Prompt The detailed signal filtering prompt is shown in Fig. 28. sections.title: F Dataset Taxonomy Details
sections.content: Figure 30: Distribution of the final dataset. This section provides detailed definitions of the capability, domain, and task categories used to analyze VidUEU-100K. F.1 Capability Categories To improve the overall capabilities of multimodal large models, we categorize the 100K instructiontuning samples into three capability paradigms: understanding, editing, and unified. Understanding: Focuses on multimodal comprehension tasks, including fine-grained visual perception and complex reasoning over visual content. Editing: Focuses on instruction-based image editing, requiring models to modify or complete visual content according to textual instructions while preserving irrelevant visual details. Unified: Involves interleaved textimage sequences, requiring the model to jointly perform multimodal understanding and generation capabilities within unified stream. F.2 Domain Categories To ensure balanced representation of both naturalistic and digitally synthesized environments, we classify the dataset into five thematic domains based on contextual semantics. Within each domain, we maximize content diversity to mitigate representation bias and ensure broad generalization. Technology & Tutorial: This category includes instructional demonstrations, software interfaces, scientific knowledge, and procedural workflows. 49 Sports & Action: This category covers athletic competitions, physical training, outdoor sports, and various dynamic action sequences. Daily Life & Human Activities: This category encompasses routine human activities, including domestic tasks, commuting, and social interactions. Nature & Scenery: This category includes natural landscapes, meteorological phenomena, and various flora and fauna. Gaming & ACG: This category consists of gameplay recordings, digital animations, comics, and interactive interface content. F.3 Task Categories Based on the generated metadata, the agent adaptively determines and generates nine task types. The first three tasks belong to Understanding, the fourth corresponds to Editing, and the final five fall under Unified. Fine-grained Perception: Requires the identification of microscopic visual details, including object attributes, existence, cardinality, and precise spatial arrangements within visual scenes. Visual Reasoning: Requires inferring logical dependencies, causal relationships, and relational dynamics between subjects across visual contexts. Multi-Image Logic: Requires maintaining coherent co-reference and logical consistency across sequence of incrementally introduced images. Editing: Requires completing missing visual content or editing existing images according to textual instructions and provided visual context. Grounded Edit-to-Select Generation: Requires generating target visual state from grounded sourcetarget changes and selecting the candidate image that matches the intended edit. Interleaved UnderstandRecallGenerateSelect: Requires extracting visible facts from earlier visual context, recalling later state, generating the recalled visual state, and selecting the matching candidate frame. Stepwise Sequence Generate-and-Select: Requires decomposing coherent visual process into ordered steps, generating intermediate visual states, and selecting candidates that match each step. Middle-Step Gap Generate-and-Fill: Requires reasoning over earlier and later frames to infer, generate, and select the missing middle visual state. Instructional Sequential Generate-and-Select: Requires inferring future visual changes from context frames, generating stepwise future states, and selecting candidates that satisfy each predicted step. F.4 Data Statistics The VidUEU dataset contains 100,000 instruction samples, comprising 40,000 understanding samples, 30,000 editing samples, and 30,000 unified interleaved multimodal generation samples. The dataset is derived from 8,268 raw videos, covering approximately 224.2 hours of measurable segment-level video duration and containing approximately 8,505 semantic segments. The detailed distributions of capabilities, domains, and task types are shown in Figure 30. F.5 Intrinsic Data-Quality Audit We randomly sampled 800 instances for human evaluation, with 200 instances per quality dimension. Two annotators independently rated each instance on 05 scale. Table 11 reports the annotator scores, their means, and Cohens κ for inter-annotator agreement. The first three dimensions were assessed at the metadata level, while editing-sample validity was evaluated at the individual editing-instruction level. sections.title: I Broader Impacts
sections.content: VidUEU-Agent and VidUEU-100K may help reduce the cost of constructing high-quality multimodal instruction data and support the development of models with stronger understanding, editing, and unified capabilities. However, even with careful human screening, source videos may contain social biases, privacy-sensitive content, or copyright risks, which may still be inherited by the constructed dataset and downstream models. Therefore, future use of VidUEU-Agent should include careful data filtering, license review, privacy protection, and safeguards against malicious use.

sections.title: J Limitations
sections.content: Although VidUEU-Agent covers multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks, it does not explicitly construct pure text-to-image generation data. This is because the advantage of video sources lies in temporal continuity and state transitions; for pure text-to-image generation, which mainly requires isolated textimage alignment, directly curating image data would be more suitable and less costly than using videos as the primary source. In addition, due to limited computational and annotation resources, we scale the dataset to 100K instruction samples, which remains modest compared with web-scale multimodal corpora. larger-scale version may further improve data diversity, long-tail coverage, and the stability of multimodal training.
